decision:is-the-economy-booming.question: Is the US economy booming, and are workers' paychecks keeping up?
decision:is-the-economy-booming.title: Is the Economy Booming, or Just Growing?
alternates: The Economy Is Growing. Why Are Paychecks Falling Behind?
Growth, Jobs and Real Wages in 2026
decision:is-the-economy-booming.whyWatch: One side says the economy is booming, the other says families are worse off, and both point at real numbers. GDP, the jobs report and real earnings show which parts of each claim hold.
decision:is-the-economy-booming.tension: GDP is growing and unemployment is low, yet real hourly pay fell over the past year. A booming economy and shrinking paychecks sound incompatible, but they are measuring different things.
decision:is-the-economy-booming.evidenceNeeded: Official GDP growth, unemployment and payroll figures for 2026, and real average hourly earnings over the past year and at the start of 2026.
decision:is-the-economy-booming.premise: Real GDP grew at 2.5% and 2.2% annual rates in the first two quarters of 2026, about trend growth: solid expansion rather than a boom. Unemployment was 4.2% in September and has stayed between 4.1% and 4.3% since March, a low rate, but payroll growth was weak (+29,000 in September) and the jobs report does not define full employment, so 'full employment' is a judgement, not a measurement. Real average hourly earnings rose 1.2% in the year to January 2026, then turned negative from April and were down 0.7% in the year to September as prices rose 3.7% and pay 3.0%. These are averages for all employees, not the median worker. So growth and falling real pay coexisted in 2026, but on the employment side it was steady rather than strong.

arc.hook: The economy grew every quarter this year, and the average worker's pay bought less in September than a year earlier.
arc.conflict: Supporters call it a boom; critics say households are going backwards. Each cites a real statistic.
arc.evidence: GDP growth against trend, the unemployment rate and payroll growth, then real hourly earnings in January and September 2026.
arc.resolution: The economy is growing at about its usual pace, not booming. Unemployment is low but hiring is slow. Real pay rose into early 2026 and has fallen since prices jumped in the spring.
arc.takeaway: When someone says the economy is booming, ask which number: output, jobs or what a paycheck buys. In 2026 they point in different directions.

coherence.reason: One question, who pays for tariffs and do they raise prices, answered by incidence, pass-through to consumer and domestic prices, how fast it arrives, and whether the effect is one-off. Whether tariffs make the country wealthier is a different question with no study.

decision:do-tariffs-raise-prices.question: Who actually pays for tariffs, and do they raise the prices Americans pay?
decision:do-tariffs-raise-prices.title: Who Really Pays for Tariffs?
alternates: Do Tariffs Raise Prices? What the 2025 Data Show
Tariffs: Do Foreign Exporters Pay, or Do We?
decision:do-tariffs-raise-prices.whyWatch: Politicians say foreign countries pay the tariffs; critics say consumers do. New York Fed research on the 2025 tariffs measured where the cost actually landed and how much reached store shelves.
decision:do-tariffs-raise-prices.tension: If foreign exporters cut their prices to keep selling, Americans pay nothing extra. If they do not, the cost lands on US importers and then on shoppers, including for goods made at home.
decision:do-tariffs-raise-prices.evidenceNeeded: Import-price data on how much of the 2025 tariffs foreign exporters absorbed, estimates of pass-through to consumer prices for imported and domestic goods, and how the effect evolves over time.
decision:do-tariffs-raise-prices.premise: Foreign exporters absorbed little of the 2025 tariffs: US importers bore about 94% of the incidence from January to August 2025 and 86% by November, according to New York Fed import-price regressions. Of a tariff increase, about 26% reached consumer goods prices within a year, and not at once: about half of the direct effect is in shop prices after three months and all of it by six, while surveyed firms describe fixed-price contracts and deliberately gradual increases, so retailers do not reprice the moment a tariff is announced. About a third of the consumer price effect came through domestically made goods, as US producers paid more for imported inputs and faced less competition. These are estimates relative to less-exposed goods, covering goods only, and they leave out the exchange rate and monetary policy. Over time the tariff effect raised the goods price level by close to 3% at its February 2026 peak and stays positive, while its contribution to twelve-month inflation is forecast to fade, so tariffs look like a rise in the level of prices more than lasting inflation; but business surveys find firms spreading increases over long periods, so in practice the one-time rise is drawn out, especially when tariffs keep changing.

arc.hook: A tariff is a tax paid at the US border. The fight is over who ends up carrying it.
arc.conflict: One side says foreign exporters cut their prices and eat the cost; the other says Americans pay it all at the checkout.
arc.evidence: The New York Fed's incidence estimates, then the pass-through to consumer prices for imported and domestic goods, then the price level against the inflation rate over time.
arc.resolution: US importers paid most of the 2025 tariffs, and part of that cost reached consumer prices, including for goods made at home. The effect raises the price level and fades from the inflation rate, but slowly.
arc.takeaway: A tariff that foreign sellers do not absorb is paid at home, by firms first and shoppers over the following year.

coherence.reason: One question, how high inflation is right now, answered against zero, the Fed target, history (in January 2026 and now), the 2022 peak and January 2025, plus the common confusion between a falling rate and falling prices.

decision:how-high-is-inflation.question: How high is US inflation right now, compared with the target, the past and the 2022 peak?
decision:how-high-is-inflation.title: How High Is Inflation, Really?
alternates: Is There Really No Inflation? The September 2026 Numbers
Inflation in 2026: High, Low, or Neither?
decision:how-high-is-inflation.whyWatch: People are told there is no inflation, that it is low by historical standards, and that it is far below the peak. The official CPI shows which of these comparisons hold and which pick a convenient baseline.
decision:how-high-is-inflation.tension: Inflation is less than half its 2022 peak, which lets one side call it low. It is also higher than when the administration took office and has been above target for five years, which lets the other side call it high.
decision:how-high-is-inflation.evidenceNeeded: The latest monthly and twelve-month CPI readings, the recent three-month pace, the CPI history back to before the pandemic, and the 2022 peak.
decision:how-high-is-inflation.premise: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September 2026 and 3.7% over twelve months, so the claim that there is no inflation is wrong. 3.7% is below the 9.1% peak of June 2022 but above every reading in 2024 and 2025, above the roughly 1.5-2.5% pace before the pandemic, and above the 3.0% of January 2025. It was a different story in January 2026: 2.4%, tied for the lowest reading since early 2021 and about the pre-pandemic pace, so 'low by historical standards' was fair then (in a series that starts in 2019) and stopped being fair by September. Prices rose about 1.1% from June to September, a 4.6% annualized pace, so the recent three months were not below target. The twelve-month CPI rate has been at least 2.3% every month since March 2021; the Fed's 2% target is defined on a different index (PCE), which usually runs somewhat lower, so 'above target' is shown on CPI. And a falling inflation rate does not mean falling prices: from January 2023 to September 2024 the rate fell from 6.4% to 2.4% while the price level kept rising.

arc.hook: Depending on who you listen to, there is no inflation, or it is the worst in years. Both cannot be right.
arc.conflict: Each side picks a baseline: the 2022 peak makes today look low; January 2025 and the Fed target make it look high.
arc.evidence: The September 2026 CPI, then the same number against history, the peak, January 2025, the recent three months and the target, then the rate against the price level.
arc.resolution: Inflation is 3.7%: far below the 2022 peak, but above target, above the start of 2025 and above any year from 2024 to 2025, and not zero by any measure.
arc.takeaway: When you hear an inflation comparison, ask what it is being compared with, and remember that a lower rate still means higher prices.

decision:how-high-is-inflation.chainWhy: Once the viewer knows inflation is back up at 3.7%, the next thing they ask is what is pushing it up: gasoline, tariffs or everything.

coherence.reason: One question, what is pushing inflation up in 2026, answered by energy, the spread beyond energy, core and shelter, and tariffs. The claim that it is a temporary by-product of the war has no study and is dropped; the pre-war trend replaces it.

decision:what-is-driving-it.question: What is pushing US inflation up in 2026: gasoline, tariffs, or prices across the board?
decision:what-is-driving-it.title: What Is Really Driving Inflation in 2026?
alternates: Is It Just Gas? What Is Behind the 2026 Inflation Jump
Gasoline, Rent or Tariffs: Where 2026 Inflation Comes From
decision:what-is-driving-it.whyWatch: Every side has a culprit: the war and gas prices, tariffs, or prices rising everywhere. The CPI breakdown shows how much each one explains.
decision:what-is-driving-it.tension: If gasoline explains the rise, it should fade when fuel prices fall. If prices have broadened, or tariffs are feeding core inflation, it will not.
decision:what-is-driving-it.evidenceNeeded: The CPI breakdown by component for September 2026, the headline and core path through 2026, shelter inflation, and estimates of the tariff contribution.
decision:what-is-driving-it.premise: Headline inflation fell to 2.4% in January and February 2026, then jumped to 3.3%, 3.8% and 4.2% from March to May as gasoline rose 24.9% in March alone; the CPI tables show the energy jump but do not name its cause. In September, gasoline rose 9.1% and accounted for over half of the monthly increase. Outside energy, many major indexes rose in September (used cars, airline fares, medical care, apparel), but core inflation was 2.6% over the year, so increases have spread without core accelerating sharply. Core ran 2.4-2.9% through 2026, a little under three percent; it dipped to 2.4% in August and edged back to 2.6% in September, so 'around three and not decelerating' overstates it. Shelter rose 3.2%, faster than core. The New York Fed estimates tariffs added about 2.9 points to twelve-month inflation in the sampled consumer goods by February 2026; that is a relative effect on goods, not a measure of core CPI, so tariffs measurably raised goods prices but their share of core inflation is not pinned down.

arc.hook: Inflation was 2.4% in February. By May it was 4.2%. What changed?
arc.conflict: One side blames gasoline and the war, another blames tariffs, and a third says prices are rising everywhere.
arc.evidence: The headline path through 2026, the gasoline share of the September rise, core and shelter, then the tariff estimate and its limits.
arc.resolution: Gasoline drove most of the jump in headline inflation. Core inflation sits a little under three percent with shelter above it, and tariffs pushed up goods prices by an amount researchers can measure only relative to less-exposed goods.
arc.takeaway: Watch core inflation, not the headline: it tells you whether the rise will outlast fuel prices.

decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.question: Is gas cheaper now than it was under Biden?
decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.title: Is Gas Cheaper Now Than Under Biden?
alternates: Gas Prices Then and Now: It Depends Which Month You Pick
Cheaper Gas? What the Pump Price Record Shows
decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.whyWatch: The claim was true for a while and then stopped being true, and people still repeat it both ways. The EIA's monthly price record shows exactly when it flipped and what drove it.
decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.tension: Gas was cheaper through 2025 and into early 2026 than the Biden-era average. Then it jumped in March 2026. Which statement is 'now' depends on the month.
decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.evidenceNeeded: Monthly US regular gasoline prices for 2021-2026, the average and peak over the previous administration, weekly prices around March 2026, and crude oil prices over the same period.
decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.premise: Over February 2021 to January 2025 regular gasoline averaged $3.46 a gallon, peaking at $4.93 in June 2022. Through 2025 it averaged $3.10, below that average every month, though about level with the last months of the previous administration; it was $2.89 in December 2025 and $2.81 and $2.91 in January and February 2026. Then it jumped: from $3.02 in the first week of March 2026 to $4.50 by mid-May, and the monthly average was $4.48 in May and $4.36 in September, well above the Biden-era average though below the 2022 peak. Crude oil moved with it: WTI averaged $97 in September 2026 against a Biden-era average of about $80. Pump prices tracked crude under both administrations, which supports the view that gas follows the world oil market, and the March jump coincides with the Iran conflict; both rest on timing and co-movement in price series, which cannot rule out other causes. All prices are nominal.

arc.hook: Gas is cheaper than under Biden: true in January 2026, false by April.
arc.conflict: Supporters quote the 2025 prices; critics quote the spring and autumn of 2026. Both are reading the same EIA table.
arc.evidence: The monthly price line from 2021 to 2026 against the Biden-era average and peak, the weekly jump in March 2026, then crude oil on the same chart.
arc.resolution: Gas was cheaper than the Biden-era average through February 2026 and has been dearer since March, though still below the 2022 peak. Pump prices moved with crude both times.
arc.takeaway: A gas price claim is only as good as its date. Check the month, and check what crude did.

decision:is-gas-cheaper-than-under-biden.chainWhy: Once the viewer learns gas is no longer cheaper than under Biden, the natural next question is whether prices overall have risen less under this administration than the last.

surprise:cumulative-price-increases-unde.question: Have prices risen less under this administration than under the last one?
surprise:cumulative-price-increases-unde.title: Have Prices Risen Less Than Under Biden?
alternates: Total Price Rises: This Administration Against the Last
6% Against 21%: A Fair Comparison of Price Rises?
surprise:cumulative-price-increases-unde.whyWatch: The total price rise under each administration is a favourite talking point. The CPI confirms the gap and shows how much of it comes from comparing a shorter term with a full one.
surprise:cumulative-price-increases-unde.tension: The total rise is far smaller so far, which sounds decisive. But one term is 20 months old and the other lasted 48.
surprise:cumulative-price-increases-unde.evidenceNeeded: The CPI price level at January 2021, January 2025 and the latest month, and the annualized rate over each period.
surprise:cumulative-price-increases-unde.premise: Consumer prices rose 21.4% from January 2021 to January 2025 and 6.1% from January 2025 to September 2026. The cumulative rise is far smaller, as the claim says, but it covers 20 months against 48. Annualized, prices rose about 5.0% a year under the previous administration and 3.6% a year since, a smaller gap than the totals suggest, and the current term's figure is still being added to.

arc.hook: 21% against 6%: the numbers are right. The comparison is the problem.
arc.conflict: The totals compare a finished four-year term with one less than two years old.
arc.evidence: The CPI level at each date, the two cumulative rises, then both converted to an annual rate.
arc.resolution: Prices have risen less so far, and more slowly per year, but the annual gap is 5.0% against 3.6%, not 21% against 6%.
arc.takeaway: Compare price rises per year, not in total, when the periods are different lengths.

surprise:gasoline-prices-rise-seasonally.question: Do gas prices really go up every summer?
surprise:gasoline-prices-rise-seasonally.title: Do Gas Prices Really Rise Every Summer?
alternates: The Summer Gas Price Myth: When Prices Actually Peak
Why Gas Peaks in May, Not August
surprise:gasoline-prices-rise-seasonally.whyWatch: Every spring someone blames the summer driving season for higher gas prices. Sixteen years of EIA monthly prices show when the seasonal rise happens and when it stops.
surprise:gasoline-prices-rise-seasonally.tension: Prices do climb from winter. But if summer driving were the cause, the peak should come in July or August, and it usually does not.
surprise:gasoline-prices-rise-seasonally.evidenceNeeded: Monthly US regular gasoline prices over many years, comparing January, May and August.
surprise:gasoline-prices-rise-seasonally.premise: In the EIA's monthly record for 2010-2025, the May price was above the January price in 15 of 16 years, so there is a seasonal rise from winter into spring. But May was at or above August in 13 of those 16 years (2024: $3.60 in May against $3.39 in August), so the seasonal peak usually comes in late spring and prices plateau or drift down through the driving season itself. The claim is right that prices rise seasonally and wrong about when they top out. The price series shows the pattern, not its cause.

arc.hook: Gas goes up every summer. Except the record says it usually peaks before summer starts.
arc.conflict: The common explanation is summer road trips; the timing of the peak does not fit it well.
arc.evidence: Sixteen years of January, May and August prices side by side.
arc.resolution: Prices rise from winter into spring in nearly every year, and usually level off or ease from May to August.
arc.takeaway: If you are waiting for summer to pass before gas gets cheaper, the seasonal high has usually already come by May.

decision:the-iran-war-and-energy.question: When the Iran conflict ends, will fuel prices come back down?
decision:the-iran-war-and-energy.title: Will Gas Prices Fall When the War Ends?
alternates: Rockets and Feathers: Do Pump Prices Fall as Fast as They Rise?
After the War: What Happens to Fuel Prices
decision:the-iran-war-and-energy.research: The two central claims are forecasts (gas returning to its pre-war level, oil staying above it) with no study, and the only evidence on the up-fast-down-slow pattern is two episodes in the weekly EIA series (partly, 0.5). It needs a pass-through study of how quickly US retail gasoline and diesel follow crude down after a supply shock, or post-war price data once the conflict ends, and an energy-market analysis of the risk premium in crude after Gulf supply disruptions.

surprise:grocery-prices-down-under-curre.question: Are grocery prices actually coming down?
surprise:grocery-prices-down-under-curre.title: Are Grocery Prices Really Coming Down?
alternates: Grocery Prices: Falling, Flat or Still Rising?
Why Your Grocery Bill Has Not Gone Back Down
surprise:grocery-prices-down-under-curre.whyWatch: Some say grocery prices are down; shoppers say their bill is not. The CPI food figures show what happened in 2025, what changed in 2026, and why a slower rate does not bring old prices back.
surprise:grocery-prices-down-under-curre.tension: Grocery prices have barely moved in recent months, which sounds like good news. But they rose through 2025 and sit far above where they were in 2020.
surprise:grocery-prices-down-under-curre.evidenceNeeded: The CPI food and food-at-home indexes through 2025 and 2026, monthly and over twelve months, and the price level against 2020.
surprise:grocery-prices-down-under-curre.premise: In 2025 food prices rose, not fell: the CPI food index was up 2.5% from January to December 2025 and 3.1% over the year to December. That index covers all food, including restaurant meals, not groceries alone. In 2026 grocery inflation slowed sharply: food at home changed -0.1%, 0.0% and -0.1% in July, August and September, so 'flat to falling' fits recent months, but grocery prices were still up 1.8% over the year to September. And a slower rate leaves the level high: by December 2025 the food index was 27% above December 2020.

arc.hook: Grocery prices are down, says one side. Then why is the bill still higher than last year?
arc.conflict: Both are reading real numbers: one the last three months, the other the last year and the last five.
arc.evidence: The food index through 2025, food at home month by month in 2026, then the level against 2020.
arc.resolution: Food prices rose in 2025. Grocery prices have been flat to slightly down since July 2026 but are still higher than a year ago, and well above 2020.
arc.takeaway: A flat month is not a lower bill. Ask whether a claim is about the last month, the last year, or the price level.

surprise:diesel-prices-reached-record-hi.question: Did diesel prices hit a record high during the Iran conflict?
surprise:diesel-prices-reached-record-hi.title: Did Diesel Hit a Record in 2026?
alternates: Record Diesel Prices? Not When People Said
Diesel in 2026: How High Did It Really Go?
surprise:diesel-prices-reached-record-hi.whyWatch: Diesel moves the price of nearly everything trucked, and the record claim was made in the spring. The monthly price record shows the claim came too early, then came true.
surprise:diesel-prices-reached-record-hi.tension: In the spring, diesel was near but below its 2022 high. By September it had passed it.
surprise:diesel-prices-reached-record-hi.evidenceNeeded: Monthly US diesel retail prices for 2022 and 2026, with the previous record month.
surprise:diesel-prices-reached-record-hi.premise: US diesel averaged $3.72 a gallon in February 2026, then $4.92 in March and $5.60 in May, the spring high, still below the June 2022 record of $5.75. The record came later: $6.29 in September 2026, 69% above February. These are nominal monthly averages, not adjusted for inflation. The rise coincides with the March 2026 crude spike and the Iran conflict; the price series shows the timing, not the cause, and does not cover heating oil.

arc.hook: In May people said diesel had hit a record. It had not, yet.
arc.conflict: Spring headlines called it a record; the monthly series had it just under 2022.
arc.evidence: Monthly diesel prices in 2022 and 2026 on one chart, with the 2022 high marked.
arc.resolution: Diesel did not set a record in the spring, but it did in September 2026, in nominal dollars.
arc.takeaway: A record claim needs a date and a measure: monthly or weekly, nominal or inflation-adjusted.
